name: PICA cerebellar infarction with mass effect
presentation: A patient develops vertigo, vomiting, headache and an unsteady gait, veering to one side, with nystagmus and dysmetria of the limbs on that side, and is initially labeled as having labyrinthitis. Within one to three days they become drowsy, with a sixth nerve palsy and then a rising blood pressure and irregular breathing, as the swollen inferior cerebellum compresses the medulla and obstructs the fourth ventricle.

deficits.sign: Limb ataxia, gait ataxia with lateropulsion, gaze-evoked nystagmus
Vertigo and vomiting from the nodulus and flocculus
Drowsiness progressing to coma with obstructive hydrocephalus
False-localizing sixth nerve palsy and facial weakness from brainstem compression

reasoning: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the inferior surface of the cerebellar hemisphere, the tonsil and the inferior vermis in addition to the lateral medulla, and an embolus or thrombus lodging beyond the medullary branches produces a purely cerebellar infarct. Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion because the hemisphere's output crosses in the midbrain and is crossed back by the corticospinal tract to reach its own side of the body, and the inferior vermis and flocculonodular lobe give the vertigo, nystagmus and truncal imbalance. The danger of the syndrome lies not in the deficit but in the anatomy of the posterior fossa: the inferior cerebellum lies against the medulla and fourth ventricle, and as the infarct swells over the following days it pushes the tonsils into the foramen magnum and the brainstem forward, obstructing CSF outflow. The resulting hydrocephalus and medullary compression cause a stepwise decline in consciousness, cranial nerve palsies and finally cardiorespiratory arrest, which decompression can prevent. The initial similarity to vestibular neuritis, which never causes limb ataxia or a positive HINTS pattern of central type, is the diagnostic trap.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the inferior cerebellar hemisphere and tonsil, sometimes with the lateral medulla.
Compressed or obliterated fourth ventricle, effaced basal cisterns, dilated temporal horns, tonsillar descent.

mimics.name: Vestibular neuritis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Normal limb coordination, positive head impulse test, unidirectional nystagmus

mimics.name: Cerebellar hemorrhage
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hyperdense on CT from the outset

mimics.name: Lateral medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bulbar signs and crossed sensory loss without significant hemispheric swelling

management: Admit to a monitored bed; repeat CT at any decline in consciousness
Suboccipital decompressive craniectomy and external ventricular drainage for deterioration from mass effect
Antithrombotic therapy and vertebral artery imaging
